title: Judgment and Hope for Egypt
overview: Isaiah describes Egypt falling apart under God's judgment, then ends with a surprising picture of Egypt and Assyria worshiping the LORD, with Israel joining them as a blessing to the world.

parts.label: The LORD comes to Egypt (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Judah's leaders often looked to Egypt for military help, so this shows that powerful ally collapsing, its gods helpless, its people fighting each other and turning to mediums. Scholars are unsure who the harsh ruler in verse 4 is; suggestions include an Assyrian king or a later Egyptian ruler who seized power.

parts.label: The Nile dries up (vv. 5-10)
parts.note: Egypt's food and jobs depended on the Nile flooding each year, so a failed river meant ruined fields and famine. Fishermen, flax workers and the weavers of Egypt's famous fine linen all lose their living.

parts.label: Wise advisers made fools (vv. 11-15)
parts.note: Zoan and Memphis were royal cities, and Egypt's advisers boasted of ancient wisdom and noble ancestry, yet they cannot see what God has planned and stagger like drunks. The pairs of head and tail, tall palm branch and lowly reed, mean everyone from the top of society to the bottom is helpless.

parts.label: Egypt trembles (vv. 16-17)
parts.note: God's raised hand is a picture of judgment about to fall. Why small Judah would frighten Egypt is unclear; some link it to Judah's ties with Assyria at the time, others to Egypt remembering that Judah's prophets had warned of this.

parts.label: Egypt turns to the LORD (vv. 18-22)
parts.note: Speaking "the language of Canaan" (Hebrew) and building an altar and memorial pillar picture Egyptians worshiping Israel's God, who answers their cries the way he once rescued Israel. Ancient manuscripts differ on one city's name, reading either "City of the Sun" or "City of Destruction."

parts.label: A highway between enemies (vv. 23-25)
parts.note: Egypt and Assyria, the two empires that had threatened Israel, are joined by a road and worship together, with Israel as the third partner, a blessing to the earth. God calls Egypt "my people" and Assyria the work of his hands, language usually kept for Israel.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the closing hope for Egypt and Assyria was fulfilled in history, such as through later Jewish and Christian communities in Egypt, or still points to a future time when nations turn to God.
think: Is there a group you find hard to imagine sharing a good future with, and what would have to change for that to seem possible?
